Paired observations instead use differences, not the independent-samples formula. State which population difference is first minus second so that the sign of the statistic matches the alternative.

blocks.title: Compute a known-variance comparison
blocks.text: Original illustration: independent samples have means 54 and 50, n1=n2=25 and known σ1=σ2=5. SE=√(25/25+25/25)=√2. Against Δ0=0, z=4/√2≈2.8284. A two-sided 5% test rejects because |z|>1.96. A causal interpretation still requires suitable assignment, not merely a small p-value.

blocks.title: Check before moving on
blocks.text: T114 has misprinted standard-error terms and T116 a pooled-variance arithmetic error. Use the formulas and recalculated numbers above.

source_reference: STA121-T38-L02; Source: T113-116 | Course topic 7

module_title: Tests for one and two proportions
title: Test a single population proportion
objective: Explain and apply test a single population proportion.

blocks.text: With x successes out of n independent Bernoulli observations, estimate p by phat=x/n. Under H0: p=p0, z=(phat-p0)/√[p0(1-p0)/n]. Use the null value p0 in the test SE. A normal approximation needs adequate expected success and failure counts; this pack uses np0≥10 and n(1-p0)≥10 as a conservative classroom check. Small counts call for an appropriate exact or other method.

blocks.title: Correct the source gambler test
blocks.text: T118-119 gives n=100, x=65 and p0=0.60, testing for any change. phat=0.65. Null SE=√(0.6×0.4/100)≈0.0489898. z=0.05/0.0489898≈1.0206. Since |z|<1.96, fail to reject at 5%. The source substitutes phat in the SE and reports a slightly different statistic; its final lack of evidence for change remains the same.

source_reference: STA121-T39-L01; Source: T116-120 | Course topic 8

module_title: Tests for one and two proportions
title: Compare two independent proportions
objective: Use compare two independent proportions to solve and interpret a specified problem.

blocks.text: Under H0: p1=p2, pool phat=(x1+x2)/(n1+n2). The test SE is √[phat(1-phat)(1/n1+1/n2)] and z=(phat1-phat2)/SE. Check independence within and between samples and adequate expected counts. A confidence interval for the difference uses an unpooled SE instead; do not reuse the null pooling mechanically.

blocks.title: Compare the source bolt proportions
blocks.text: T120 has x1=30,n1=1000 and x2=100,n2=1200. Estimates are 0.03 and 0.0833333. Pooled phat=130/2200≈0.0590909. SE≈0.0100961 and z≈-5.2826. A two-sided 5% test rejects equality. Report the estimated difference -0.0533333, about -5.33 percentage points, alongside the statistical result.

blocks.title: Check before moving on
blocks.text: T117 prints n1+n1 in the pooled denominator; it must be n1+n2. Hypothesis-test standard errors and confidence-interval standard errors serve different purposes.

source_reference: STA121-T39-L02; Source: T116-120 | Course topic 8

module_title: Point estimation and properties of estimators
title: Distinguish estimator, estimate and parameter
objective: Explain and apply distinguish estimator, estimate and parameter.

blocks.text: A parameter is a fixed unknown population quantity in the frequentist framework used here. An estimator is a rule based on a random sample; its realised numerical value is an estimate. The sample mean estimates μ and the sample proportion estimates p. Point estimation gives one number; interval estimation gives a range produced by a procedure with a specified coverage rate. An estimate should be accompanied by information about uncertainty.

blocks.title: Separate a rule from its value
blocks.text: For a random sample X1,...,Xn, the estimator mean(X) is random before observations. After values 4,6,8 are observed, its estimate is 6. The population μ remains fixed and unknown. Repeating the sample may produce another mean. A 95% procedure describes how often intervals constructed by the rule cover μ, not how often μ changes.

source_reference: STA121-T40-L01; Source: T121-124 | Course topic 9

module_title: Point estimation and properties of estimators
title: Compare estimator properties
objective: Use compare estimator properties to solve and interpret a specified problem.

blocks.text: Unbiasedness means E(estimator)=parameter. Consistency means convergence in probability to the parameter as n grows. Among unbiased estimators of the same parameter, lower variance gives greater efficiency in that comparison. Sufficiency means the statistic retains all information in the sample about the parameter under the specified model. No single observed estimate demonstrates unbiasedness; the property concerns repeated-sample behaviour.

blocks.title: Compare unbiased estimators
blocks.text: Original illustration: two unbiased estimators of μ have variances 4 and 9 under the same model and sample size. The first is more efficient by the smaller-variance criterion. An estimator with constant bias 1 and variance tending to zero is not consistent for μ: it concentrates near μ+1. Bias, variance and consistency are different properties.

blocks.title: Check before moving on
blocks.text: T124 conflates a chosen significance level with an observed p-value. Keep α fixed by design and p-value calculated from the data and test model.

source_reference: STA121-T40-L02; Source: T121-124 | Course topic 9

module_title: Confidence intervals for means and proportions
title: Interpret and construct intervals
objective: Explain and apply interpret and construct intervals.

blocks.text: A confidence interval has form estimate ± critical multiplier×SE. The margin of error is the multiplier times SE; width is twice that margin. For a normal population with known σ, mean CI is mean±z(1-α/2)σ/√n. With unknown σ, use mean±t(1-α/2,n-1)s/√n under the t-model assumptions. Higher confidence requires a wider interval for the same data. Frequentist confidence refers to long-run coverage of the procedure.

blocks.title: Construct the source voter interval
blocks.text: T133 has 600 of 800 voters in a category. phat=0.75. SE=√(0.75×0.25/800)≈0.0153093. A 95% Wald margin is 1.96×SE≈0.0300062. Interval=(0.719994,0.780006), about 72.00%-78.00%. The method assumes an appropriate random design and approximate independence; the interval does not repair selection bias.

source_reference: STA121-T41-L01; Source: T125-128, T132-133 | Course topic 10

module_title: Confidence intervals for means and proportions
title: Proportions and differences
objective: Use proportions and differences to solve and interpret a specified problem.

blocks.text: A large-sample Wald interval for one proportion is phat±z√[phat(1-phat)/n], using adequate successes and failures. For p1-p2 from independent samples, use difference±z√[phat1(1-phat1)/n1+phat2(1-phat2)/n2]. Wald intervals are classroom approximations and can perform poorly near 0 or 1. A pooled t interval for two means uses (mean1-mean2)±t sp√(1/n1+1/n2), when its assumptions hold.

blocks.title: Use a small-sample t interval
blocks.text: Original illustration of T127: n=16, mean=20, s=4, with a normal population and unknown σ. SE=4/4=1. A 95% critical t with df=15 is about 2.13145. Interval=20±2.13145=(17.86855,22.13145). It is wider than the z interval because σ is estimated. Do not describe this as a 95% probability that the fixed μ is in this realised interval.

blocks.title: Check before moving on
blocks.text: T126 wrongly says a general normal distribution has mean zero and variance greater than one. Only the standard normal fixes mean 0 and variance 1.

source_reference: STA121-T41-L02; Source: T125-128, T132-133 | Course topic 10

title: Plan sample size for a mean
objective: Explain and apply plan sample size for a mean.

blocks.text: For an approximate two-sided mean interval with known or defensibly planned σ and desired margin E, n=(zσ/E)², rounded up. A pilot estimate can inform planning but is not magically a known population SD. More variability or higher confidence increases n; a larger allowable error reduces it. The formula assumes a suitable sampling design and does not include design effects, nonresponse inflation or a finite-population adjustment unless explicitly added.

blocks.title: Recalculate the source ISP plan
blocks.text: T131 uses 95% confidence, σ=6.95 minutes and E=1 minute. Using z=1.96, n=(1.96×6.95/1)²=185.552644, so at least 186 randomly selected households are required under the model. Rounding to 185 would miss the target. The chosen n plans interval precision; it does not guarantee that any one sample mean is within one minute.

source_reference: STA121-T42-L01; Source: T128-133 | Course topic 11

title: Plan sample size for a proportion
objective: Use plan sample size for a proportion to solve and interpret a specified problem.

blocks.text: Use n=z²p*(1-p*)/E², with a planning proportion p*. If no prior value is available, p*=0.5 maximises p*(1-p*) and gives a conservative value. Round up. For the same confidence and variability, margin is proportional to 1/√n: quartering the margin requires 16 times the sample size. Sample-size planning should consider cost, heterogeneity, resources, purpose and precision.

blocks.title: Plan a proportion and an improvement
blocks.text: At 95% confidence with no prior p and E=0.05, n=1.96²×0.25/0.05²=384.16, so take 385. To halve E to 0.025, n=1536.64, so take 1537. The underlying unrounded requirement quadruples. If 80% response is anticipated, inviting ceil(385/0.8)=482 is a separate operational allowance, not a cure for nonresponse bias.

blocks.title: Check before moving on
